opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of those questions where the answer has changed over time, and people's intuitions haven't fully caught up.

If you go back to the early days, a lot of the most important ideas in deep learning were discovered with very little compute. AlexNet was trained on two GPUs. The transformer paper used, by today's standards, a pretty modest amount. Many of the ideas that ended up mattering most were demonstrated at small scale first. That tells you something: to show an idea is real, you don't necessarily need the biggest cluster in the world. You need enough to convince yourself and others that there's a signal.

Building the best system is a different activity. Once you know what you want to do, scaling it up, making it robust, squeezing out every bit of performance, takes an enormous amount of compute. A large part of that compute goes into the final training runs, but also into all the experiments around them that make sure those runs work.

So the research compute and the frontier-system compute are related, but they're not the same thing. I'd say research needs *enough* compute, not *the most* compute. The bottleneck in research is more often ideas than raw FLOPs. You need to be able to run experiments at a scale where the results are informative, where you're not fooling yourself because something only works when the model is tiny. That bar has gone up, but it's still well below what it takes to train the best model.

There's also something subtle. When everyone has a lot of compute, and everyone is doing roughly the same thing, the differentiator becomes ideas again. In the scaling era there was a very clear recipe: get more data, more compute, bigger model, and things improve. That recipe was so effective that it absorbed much of the field's attention. But as you push it further, the question becomes: what else? And when you're asking "what else," you're back in research mode, where taste and insight count for at least as much as the size of your cluster.

So my short answer: building the best system takes vastly more compute than doing good research. But good research still needs a meaningful amount, enough to test ideas at a scale where they're believable, and the people who use their compute most thoughtfully will have an advantage.

r001.rationale: It says research needs “enough” compute, “not the most,” and that this is below what it takes to train the best model.

r002.rationale: It describes a scaling recipe where more compute improves results, but does not clearly identify compute as a differentiator among systems following the same paradigm. It instead says ideas become the differentiator when compute is widely available.

fable-5.1.text:
I think these are really different regimes, and it's important not to conflate them.

Building the best system at any given moment is dominated by scale. You take the recipe that works, you run it on as much compute as you can get, and you push data and parameters and training length as far as the budget allows. That's an enormous amount of compute, and the number is set mostly by economics, not by science. Whoever has the most chips, roughly, has the biggest model.

Research is different. The purpose of research is to find out whether an idea is right, and most ideas can be tested at a much smaller scale than the frontier. If something is going to help, you can usually see the signal at a size that's a hundred or a thousand times smaller than the largest run. Not always, and some things only show up at scale, which is the frustrating part. But the bulk of the learning happens in experiments that are small by today's standards. What matters more there is how many experiments you can run and how good your taste is about which experiments to run. Compute helps, but it's the number of ideas you get to try, and the quality of the people deciding, that dominates.

So my view is that the compute for research is a modest fraction of the compute for the final system, but it's compute that is used very differently. The big run is one shot. Research is thousands of small shots, and the thing you are optimizing is the rate at which you learn something true. I'd actually say that over the past few years the field has over-indexed on the first regime and under-invested in the second, and as the easy scaling gains get harder to find, the balance is going to shift back toward research.

r001.rationale: It says most research ideas can be tested at much smaller scale than the frontier and that research compute is a modest fraction of the final system’s compute.

r002.rationale: It says building the best system uses the working recipe at the largest affordable scale and that whoever has the most chips roughly has the biggest model, identifying compute scale as a major differentiator.

astra-6.text:
I think those can be quite different. If you know exactly what you want to build, and you want to build the best possible system, then you may need an enormous amount of compute. But if you’re doing research, you’re asking: is there a better way to do this? And you can often test an idea at a much smaller scale.

The difficulty is that not every idea that works at a small scale will work at a large scale. So you need enough compute to convince yourself that the thing you’ve discovered is real and will carry over. That can still be substantial. But it’s different from needing to run the largest training run in the world.

So I would distinguish between the compute needed to discover something and the compute needed to fully exploit that discovery.

r001.rationale: The response says research ideas can often be tested at a much smaller scale and distinguishes discovery from running the largest training run.

r002.rationale: It contrasts research compute with compute for building the best system, but does not say compute is a major differentiator among systems developed within the same paradigm.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those can be quite different. If you want to build the best system using an approach that already works, then having more compute is a very direct advantage. You can train a bigger model, run more experiments, and push the approach further.

Research is a little different, because you’re trying to discover something that you don’t yet know how to do. You need enough compute to test your ideas, but the most important experiment may be much smaller than the final training run. A good idea can sometimes be demonstrated at a relatively modest scale.

The complication is that some ideas only reveal their value at scale. So I wouldn’t say compute is unimportant for research. The question is whether you have enough to distinguish a promising idea from a bad one. That could be substantially less than what you need to build the very best system.

r001.rationale: It says the compute needed to test a research idea could be substantially less than what is needed to build the very best system.

r002.rationale: It says that when using an approach that already works, more compute is a direct advantage, enabling larger models and more experiments.
